summary: Implements a binary search to locate the first occurrence of a target integer in a sorted list of integers, returning its index or -1 if absent.
input_domain: Sorted lists of integers (arr) and integer values (x)

items.behavior: Find first occurrence of x in middle with duplicates
items.rationale: Spec example and requirement: 'The lowest index i such that arr[i] == x'

items.behavior: Find first occurrence at the start of the list
items.rationale: Spec requires the lowest index; duplicates at the beginning should yield index 0

items.behavior: Find first occurrence at the end of the list
items.rationale: Spec requires the lowest index; when duplicates occupy the tail, the first index of the block is returned
Spec states '-1 if x not in arr'; an empty list contains no elements

items.behavior: Single element list with exact match
items.rationale: Spec states lowest index i where arr[i]==x; a single matching element returns 0
Spec states '-1 if x not in arr'

items.behavior: Target x is smaller than all elements
items.rationale: Spec states '-1 if x not in arr'; binary search must correctly handle underflow conditions

items.behavior: Target x is larger than all elements
items.rationale: Spec states '-1 if x not in arr'; binary search must correctly handle overflow conditions

items.behavior: All elements in list are equal to x
items.rationale: Spec requires the lowest index; when every element matches, index 0 is correct

items.behavior: Target x is absent but falls between existing values
items.rationale: Spec states '-1 if x not in arr'

ambiguities: Behavior when `arr` violates the implicit precondition of being sorted (spec defines it as a sorted list but does not specify error handling for unsorted inputs)
Type enforcement for non-integer elements in `arr` or non-integer `x` (spec restricts to ints but does not state whether to raise TypeError, coerce, or ignore)
Handling of negative indices or out-of-bounds access (Python's default wrapping/indexing vs spec intent)
Expected time/space complexity guarantees beyond the implied O(log n) from 'Binary Search'
